title: Anxiety (IV.11)
hookLine: Francis de Sales calls anxiety the worst evil after sin; is it a failing to fix, or a weight to carry?
tomorrow: why would a saint tell you to redo your resolutions every year?

cards: The essay's due Friday. The first sentence has been rewritten so many times it no longer means anything, and it's one a.m., and the heart won't slow down. Here's Francis de Sales's answer to yesterday's question.

Apart from sin, he writes, anxiety is the greatest evil that can come to a soul. That lands hard on anyone who has lain awake with a racing heart they never chose. So which is it: a failing to fix, or a weight to carry?
Catholics give more than one answer.

teach.b: Hear Francis first. Anxiety, he says, is born of a restless desire to be free of some trouble, or to gain some good, and to have it now. The wanting isn't the problem.
The thrashing is. He pictures a bird caught in a net: every beat of its wings ties it tighter. A troubled heart loses its strength in the struggle, and its judgment with it.
So seek the help you need, he says, but calmly, trusting God more than your own speed.
He borrows a line from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "My soul is continually in my hands." Keep checking that it still is. Now the other voice, heard among Catholics today.
Much anxiety isn't chosen. It lives in the body, and calling it an evil can pile guilt on top of fear.

teach.h: NOT CHOSEN: A WEIGHT, NOT A FAULT.
teach.b: Treat it as a weight to carry with help, not a fault. Here's where the two meet. Francis never says just stop feeling it.

teach.h: SAY IT TO A FAITHFUL FRIEND.
teach.b: He says tell the anxiety to a spiritual director or a faithful friend, because it eases when it's spoken.
Asking for help is the calm move, not the thrashing one. If worry ever turns into thoughts of harming yourself, reach out now: in the US, call or text 988, or call your local emergency number.

how: Catholics bring worries to God in prayer and some talk them over with a priest, a spiritual director or a trusted friend; for anxiety that weighs heavily, some also seek medical or counseling help.

o: a feeling that proves you've done wrong
a sensible plan for future problems
a restless worry that tangles the soul

p: someone to say the worry to

s: for Francis, wanting relief from a trouble is the problem
the wanting is fine. the restless thrashing for it, now, is what tangles the soul.
Francis compares an anxious heart to a bird caught in a net
every beat of its wings ties it tighter.
Francis says a devout person keeps worries to herself
he advises telling them to a spiritual director or a faithful friend.

games.q: your cousin says Francis is too harsh: her panic attacks aren't a choice, so calling anxiety an evil just adds guilt. what's her strongest point?
o: fear she didn't choose isn't a sin, and getting help isn't a lack of faith.
Francis wrote long ago, so nothing in his chapter applies now.
if anxiety isn't a choice, then nothing can be done about it.
games.why: that's her best case, and Francis leaves room for it: he ranks anxiety apart from sin and tells the anxious to seek help calmly and say it to a friend.

practice: Turn one hand palm up on your knee and set one worry in it, the way you'd hold a small bird, without squeezing. Let your shoulders drop a little with each breath out.
If you pray, you can bring it to God with the psalm: my soul is continually in my hands.

wordCard.voice: Anxiety. For Francis, a restless rush to be free of a trouble: the thrashing that only tightens the net.

carryVoice: The line to keep: don't be anxious, and seek help steadily, with your soul still in your hands. Talk soon.
